paragraphs.text: Along sheltered tropical and subtropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea, a peculiar kind of forest stands with its feet in salt water. Mangroves are not a single species but a collection of trees and shrubs, drawn from several unrelated plant families, that have independently evolved ways of surviving conditions that would kill most land plants. With each high tide, seawater floods their roots; as the tide retreats, it exposes soft, airless mud. Some species cope by filtering salt out at the roots, while others take it in and excrete it through glands on their leaves. Many send up pencil-like roots from the mud, which act as snorkels, allowing the buried root system to breathe. Others are propped up on arching stilt roots that make the forest look as though it is walking into the water.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: It is this tangle of roots and trunks that makes mangroves so valuable to the people who live behind them. When waves enter a mangrove belt, they lose energy through friction as water is forced around countless obstacles. In a study on a low-lying delta coast, coastal engineer Nirmala Seneviratne placed pressure sensors at intervals through a forest 300 metres wide and recorded conditions over two monsoon seasons. She found that the height of ordinary waves fell by around 60 per cent between the seaward edge and the landward edge. Seneviratne is careful not to overstate the result. Exceptionally powerful storm surges, she notes, can push water through even a healthy forest, and a narrow fringe of trees offers far less protection than a broad one. Nevertheless, in her view, a wide belt can do much of the work of a concrete sea wall at a fraction of the cost, and unlike a wall it repairs itself.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Mangroves also shape the land itself. Their roots slow the movement of water so that fine particles carried by rivers and tides settle out instead of being washed away. Over time this trapped sediment, together with decaying roots, raises the forest floor. Where enough sediment is available, the ground can build up quickly enough to keep pace with the rising sea, something no artificial barrier can do. The same waterlogged soils lock away remarkable quantities of carbon, because dead plant material decomposes very slowly in the absence of oxygen. Researchers have found that, area for area, mangrove forests can store several times as much carbon as many forests on dry land, mostly in their soils. The shallow channels between the roots, meanwhile, shelter young fish, shrimp and crabs, many of which are later caught by fishers once they move into open water.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Despite these benefits, mangroves have been cleared on a vast scale. A substantial share of the world's mangrove area has disappeared since the middle of the twentieth century. In parts of Southeast Asia and Latin America, a major cause was the spread of shrimp farming: forests were cut down and replaced by rectangular ponds enclosed by earth walls. Such ponds were often productive for only a few years before disease and accumulated waste forced owners to abandon them and clear new ground. Elsewhere, mangroves gave way to rice paddies, oil palm plantations, ports and tourist resorts, or were thinned for timber and charcoal. Because the forests occupied land that seemed to have no owner and no obvious use, their destruction attracted little attention until coastal communities began to notice increased flooding and smaller catches. The rate of loss has slowed considerably in recent years, partly because the value of the forests is now more widely understood.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Replanting has become popular with governments, charities and companies, but early efforts produced disappointing results. Ecologist Esteban Ruvalcaba visited 46 restoration sites along one stretch of coast and counted how many trees were still alive five years after planting. Where volunteers had pushed seedlings into open mudflats below the natural forest edge, survival was often under 10 per cent: the young trees spent too long underwater each day and were swept away or drowned. Projects that planted a single fast-growing species in neat rows did somewhat better but created plantations that supported few animals. The most successful sites, Ruvalcaba found, were abandoned shrimp ponds where the earth walls had simply been broken open. Once tidal water could flow in and out again, seeds arrived naturally from nearby forests, and after five years these sites held a richer mix of species than any of the planted ones. His conclusion is that restoring the right water conditions often matters more than planting itself.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Even a well-designed project can fail if the people living nearby see no reason to protect it. Social scientist Adaeze Nwosu compared villages where restoration had been organised by outside agencies with villages where residents had helped to choose the sites and set the rules. In the second group, young forests were far less likely to be cut down again within a decade. Nwosu points in particular to agreements that gave local families the right to collect crabs from the restored areas, which turned the forest into a source of income worth defending. Her work suggests that mangroves will only hold the line against the sea if they are also valued by those who live on the shore.
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
Mangroves on the Front Line

A. Along sheltered tropical and subtropical coastlines, where rivers meet the sea, a peculiar kind of forest stands with its feet in salt water. Mangroves are not a single species but a collection of trees and shrubs, drawn from several unrelated plant families, that have independently evolved ways of surviving conditions that would kill most land plants. With each high tide, seawater floods their roots; as the tide retreats, it exposes soft, airless mud. Some species cope by filtering salt out at the roots, while others take it in and excrete it through glands on their leaves. Many send up pencil-like roots from the mud, which act as snorkels, allowing the buried root system to breathe. Others are propped up on arching stilt roots that make the forest look as though it is walking into the water.

B. It is this tangle of roots and trunks that makes mangroves so valuable to the people who live behind them. When waves enter a mangrove belt, they lose energy through friction as water is forced around countless obstacles. In a study on a low-lying delta coast, coastal engineer Nirmala Seneviratne placed pressure sensors at intervals through a forest 300 metres wide and recorded conditions over two monsoon seasons. She found that the height of ordinary waves fell by around 60 per cent between the seaward edge and the landward edge. Seneviratne is careful not to overstate the result. Exceptionally powerful storm surges, she notes, can push water through even a healthy forest, and a narrow fringe of trees offers far less protection than a broad one. Nevertheless, in her view, a wide belt can do much of the work of a concrete sea wall at a fraction of the cost, and unlike a wall it repairs itself.

C. Mangroves also shape the land itself. Their roots slow the movement of water so that fine particles carried by rivers and tides settle out instead of being washed away. Over time this trapped sediment, together with decaying roots, raises the forest floor. Where enough sediment is available, the ground can build up quickly enough to keep pace with the rising sea, something no artificial barrier can do. The same waterlogged soils lock away remarkable quantities of carbon, because dead plant material decomposes very slowly in the absence of oxygen. Researchers have found that, area for area, mangrove forests can store several times as much carbon as many forests on dry land, mostly in their soils. The shallow channels between the roots, meanwhile, shelter young fish, shrimp and crabs, many of which are later caught by fishers once they move into open water.

D. Despite these benefits, mangroves have been cleared on a vast scale. A substantial share of the world's mangrove area has disappeared since the middle of the twentieth century. In parts of Southeast Asia and Latin America, a major cause was the spread of shrimp farming: forests were cut down and replaced by rectangular ponds enclosed by earth walls. Such ponds were often productive for only a few years before disease and accumulated waste forced owners to abandon them and clear new ground. Elsewhere, mangroves gave way to rice paddies, oil palm plantations, ports and tourist resorts, or were thinned for timber and charcoal. Because the forests occupied land that seemed to have no owner and no obvious use, their destruction attracted little attention until coastal communities began to notice increased flooding and smaller catches. The rate of loss has slowed considerably in recent years, partly because the value of the forests is now more widely understood.

E. Replanting has become popular with governments, charities and companies, but early efforts produced disappointing results. Ecologist Esteban Ruvalcaba visited 46 restoration sites along one stretch of coast and counted how many trees were still alive five years after planting. Where volunteers had pushed seedlings into open mudflats below the natural forest edge, survival was often under 10 per cent: the young trees spent too long underwater each day and were swept away or drowned. Projects that planted a single fast-growing species in neat rows did somewhat better but created plantations that supported few animals. The most successful sites, Ruvalcaba found, were abandoned shrimp ponds where the earth walls had simply been broken open. Once tidal water could flow in and out again, seeds arrived naturally from nearby forests, and after five years these sites held a richer mix of species than any of the planted ones. His conclusion is that restoring the right water conditions often matters more than planting itself.

F. Even a well-designed project can fail if the people living nearby see no reason to protect it. Social scientist Adaeze Nwosu compared villages where restoration had been organised by outside agencies with villages where residents had helped to choose the sites and set the rules. In the second group, young forests were far less likely to be cut down again within a decade. Nwosu points in particular to agreements that gave local families the right to collect crabs from the restored areas, which turned the forest into a source of income worth defending. Her work suggests that mangroves will only hold the line against the sea if they are also valued by those who live on the shore.

explanation.ru: В абзаце D утверждается, что темпы исчезновения в последнее время заметно замедлились, то есть леса пропадают медленнее, чем раньше.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D зазначено, що темпи втрат останнім часом значно сповільнилися, тож ліси зникають повільніше, ніж раніше.
